A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSCP, SSCQL, and GC-SSCP research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison across the reorganized sections.

before.justification: V1 reports original offline RL, online adaptation, behavior-cloning, and goal-conditioned RL experiments, together with training curves and ablations.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds author-run FQL comparisons and completion-flow inference results in Appendix A.7.

M1.justification: The core architectures, training losses, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. Appendix A.7 adds an optional inference variant that integrates the trained completion field using ten Euler steps, without retraining or additional hyperparameter tuning.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same D4RL locomotion datasets, online locomotion settings, five RoboMimic tasks plus Push-T, and sixteen OGBench environment-dataset combinations. The new FQL and completion-flow experiments reuse existing locomotion tasks.

E2.justification: FQL was cited in v1 but was not an evaluated comparator. V3 adds it to Table 1 and provides a dedicated hyperparameter-tuned comparison in Table 11. The other benchmark comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V1 reports 500K fully online training steps in its results discussion and Appendix A.3, despite already specifying 2M elsewhere. V3 consistently specifies 2M in Appendix A.3–A.4 while retaining the scores; this is a reported protocol correction, not evidence of rerunning experiments. Added protocols include FQL hyperparameter selection and ten-step Euler inference.

E4.justification: V3 Table 12 newly tests whether the trained completion field supports multistep inference on six locomotion datasets, and Table 11 exposes FQL performance across regularization coefficients. The existing loss-weight, bootstrap-target, AWR-temperature, inference-type, and subgoal-interval ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Existing seed counts and uncertainty reporting remain unchanged, including three training seeds for online RL and behavior cloning, eight for GCRL, and the stated omission of repeated training seeds in the temperature sweep. The new tables add point estimates without introducing a new statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores and plotted findings are retained. V3 adds FQL results, including its 66.8 average in Table 1, and six completion-flow results in Table 12. For example, ten-step inference reports 98.0 versus 85.9 for single-step Walker2d-MR, but 94.8 versus 101.4 for Hopper-MR; these are new inference-setting comparisons, not between-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, value and advantage formulas, and time-sampling derivation are unchanged. The additional completion-flow experiment introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The central claims about expressive single-step policies, off-policy optimization, and hierarchy distilled into flat goal-conditioned policies are retained. V3 shifts abstract emphasis toward GCRL and adds an introductory summary of GCRL findings already claimed in v1 Section 5.3.

C2.justification: Appendix A.7 newly interprets multistep results as evidence that the completion field retains meaningful flow structure and supports both single-step and iterative generation. The conclusion's limitations concerning expressiveness, long horizons, regularization tuning, and continuous action spaces remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 adds a repository link for the authors' implementation and a reproducibility statement describing installation instructions and reproduction scripts. Appendix A.7 also documents the added evaluation settings, although its FQL sweep prose specifies a final alpha of 2.0 while Table 11 labels it 3.0. Existing architecture, hardware, and benchmark implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: The same 51 cited works are retained, including FQL. V3 adds a focused discussion distinguishing SSCQL from FQL through its shared generative actor, direct dataset supervision, and avoidance of full-flow training rollouts; this expands positioning relative to one existing reference.

P1.justification: Most prose is retained. V3 expands the introductory GCRL motivation, separates online experiments into their own subsection, reorganizes Appendix A, adds acknowledgment and reproducibility sections, and removes the brief Broader Impact appendix. Citation style and heading terminology also change.

P2.justification: V3 adopts ICLR title, author, header, and heading formatting while retaining all fifteen figures. It adds an FQL column to Table 1, inference-type grouping to Table 6, and new Tables 11–12. Appendix Tables 7, 8, and 15 redisplay existing main-text results; other exhibit changes mainly involve placement and emphasis.

improvement.justification: V3 improves the paper through a relevant FQL comparison, a useful test of multistep completion-field inference, implementation access information, and reconciliation of the conflicting online-training budget. These are focused gains while the core evidence remains stable. The new FQL alpha discrepancy between prose and Table 11 limits reproducibility of that comparison but does not outweigh the overall benefits.
